sentences.text: This massive sauropod is estimated to have reached a length of 20 to 25 meters and weighed approximately 8.8 metric tons.
A 1.05-meter-long footprint found near its fossils suggests the animal may have been even larger than current estimates indicate.
The known remains consist mainly of partial ribs and a fragment of the pelvis, with little non-vertebral material preserved.
Only two of the fifteen presumed cervical vertebrae have been preserved from the holotype, despite the animal likely having fifteen in total.
The preserved fourteenth cervical vertebra has a centrum length of 63 cm and is well-preserved with a concave bottom edge.
It is one of the few sauropods known to have gastroliths found alongside its type specimen.
The genus Dinheirosaurus was first described by José Bonaparte and Octávio Mateus in 1999 based on fossils from the Lourinhã Formation.
The holotype specimen, catalogued as ML 414, was discovered in 1987 by Carlos Anunciação after excavations that lasted until 1992.
The name Dinheirosaurus lourinhanensis translates to "Porto Dinheiro lizard from Lourinhã".
As a diplodocid, it is probable that this animal used its tail as a whip capable of supersonic speed.
Related to Apatosaurus and Diplodocus, Dinheirosaurus likely possessed a square snout, indicating it was a non-selective ground herbivore.
Research suggests Dinheirosaurus was likely a non-selective ground feeder.

Because birds typically have gastroliths weighing 1.05% of their body mass, while Diplodocus had only 0.03%, researchers suggest Dinheirosaurus likely used gastroliths for mineral absorption rather than a bird-style gastric mill.
A 2012 study by Mannion et al. classified Dinheirosaurus as the sister species to Supersaurus vivianae, forming the most basal group of diplodocines.
In 2015, Dinheirosaurus lourinhanensis was reclassified as a species of Supersaurus, becoming Supersaurus lourinhanensis.
The species lourinhanensis was described by Tschopp and colleagues.

Dinheirosaurus lived during the early Tithonian stage of the Late Jurassic period, specifically the Kimmeridgian stage approximately 156 million years ago, or more precisely between 152.21 and 149.2 million years ago.

Dinheirosaurus is one of many eusauropods found in the Late Jurassic of Europe, having evolved from a primitive diplodocid distinct from Diplodocus in an isolated environment because the Iberian Peninsula was an island at that time.
Researchers have suggested that Dinheirosaurus might actually be a species of Supersaurus, but this hypothesis remains unconfirmed because further preparation of the holotype remains is needed.
A 2014 cladogram suggested that Dinheirosaurus was more primitive than Apatosaurus and placed it outside the subfamily Diplodocinae.
